sections.title: Lesson 10.1: Government Regulators
sections.overview: Federal regulation of the U.S. securities industry is anchored by the SEC, created under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, with supporting roles played by Treasury branches (FinCEN, IRS, OCC), state administrators coordinated through NASAA, and the two principal insurance regimes—SIPC for broker-dealer customers and FDIC for bank depositors. Understanding each regulator's jurisdiction, the major federal securities acts, and the distinction between SIPC and FDIC coverage limits is foundational for the SIE exam.
key_concepts: SEC: primary federal securities regulator; created by the Securities Exchange Act of 1934; composed of 5 commissioners (no more than 3 from the same political party).
SEC jurisdiction: registration of broker-dealers, exchanges, trading markets, SIPs; delegates representative licensing to FINRA.

SEC enforcement powers: censure, limit activities, suspend/revoke registration (including permanent industry bar), impose fines. SEC has NO arrest power — criminal cases are referred to the Department of Justice.
A BD may not claim that SEC registration implies SEC approval of its financial standing or conduct (misrepresentation).

Security defined: an intangible financial asset that may be bought, sold, or gifted, represented by a paper certificate or electronic record. Commodities (gold, oil, beef) and futures are NOT securities.
FinCEN (Treasury): collects/analyzes financial intelligence; receives suspicious activity and large cash transaction reports under BSA/AML.
IRS (Treasury): primary federal tax enforcement; BDs must provide customer/firm information on demand.

Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC, Treasury): supervises ~1,400 national banks, federal savings associations, and U.S. branches of foreign banks; Comptroller also serves as an FDIC director. WARNING: do not confuse with Options Clearing Corporation (also abbreviated OCC).
SIPC: nonprofit membership corporation created under the Securities Investor Protection Act of 1970 (SIPA); funded by member assessments; protects customers in BD bankruptcy.
SIPC coverage: up to $500,000 per separate customer (separate capacity), of which a MAXIMUM of $250,000 may be cash.

SIPC separate capacities: individual, joint, custodial, IRA each receive separate $500,000 coverage; cash + margin accounts of same customer are COMBINED; only margin equity (not full market value) is covered.
SIPC does NOT cover: commodities, commodity futures, currency contracts/losses. Excess claims make the customer a general creditor of the BD.

SIPC membership required for all SEC-registered BDs EXCEPT: (1) banks dealing exclusively in municipal securities, (2) firms dealing exclusively in U.S. government securities, (3) firms dealing exclusively in redeemable investment company (mutual fund) securities.
SIPC disclosure: written disclosure at account opening AND annually thereafter; SIPC sign posted on premises; 'SIPC' may not appear larger than the firm's own name in advertising.
FDIC: independent federal agency insuring bank deposits; funded by premiums from member banks.
FDIC coverage: $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category.
FDIC covers: checking, savings, MMDA, CDs, self-directed IRA bank deposits. FDIC does NOT cover: mutual funds, annuities, life insurance, stocks, bonds.
Uniform Securities Act (USA, 1956): federal template adopted by all states; mandates a state securities Administrator in each state with authority over registration of securities, BDs, IAs, and reps.
NASAA: North American Securities Administrators Association — represents state/provincial regulators in U.S., Canada, Mexico; issues Model Rules; has NO independent regulatory authority.
rules: Securities Act of 1933 — primary (new issue) market; issuer registration.

Securities Exchange Act of 1934 — secondary markets; created SEC; insider transactions, short sales, proxies; customer protection rule; net capital rule; issuer reporting (e.g., annual reports); BD/exchange registration.
Investment Company Act of 1940 — mutual funds, closed-end funds, UITs.
Investment Advisers Act of 1940 — firms earning fees for investment advice.
Securities Investor Protection Act of 1970 (SIPA) — created SIPC; customer protection on BD bankruptcy.
Insider Trading and Securities Fraud Enforcement Act of 1988 — penalties for misuse of material nonpublic information.
USA PATRIOT Act of 2001 (built on Bank Secrecy Act of 1970) — AML policies/procedures.
formulas: SIPC max coverage per separate customer = $500,000 total, with cash component capped at $250,000
FDIC max coverage = $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category
Margin account SIPC coverage = equity in the account (not market value)
mnemonics: '33 = New issues; '34 = eXchanges & SEC; '40 = funds & advisers; '70 = SIPC; '88 = Insider; '01 = PATRIOT.
SIPC = Securities (BDs) | FDIC = Funds in Deposit accounts (Banks).
SIPC '5-2-5-0 / 2-5-0' — Five hundred K total, Two-Fifty cash.
OCC has two meanings: Office of Comptroller of Currency (banks) vs. Options Clearing Corporation (options) — read the question carefully.

sections.title: Lesson 10.2: Self-Regulatory Organizations (SROs)
sections.overview: SROs are industry bodies authorized by the SEC to write and enforce rules for their members. FINRA is the dominant SRO for broker-dealers and their associated persons; the MSRB writes (but does not enforce) rules for municipal securities; and the exchanges regulate trading on their own venues. This lesson also covers FINRA's four rulebooks, the disciplinary appeals chain, and SEC/FINRA record-retention requirements under Rules 17a-3 and 17a-4.
key_concepts: FINRA: successor to NASD (consolidated with NYSE Member Regulation in 2007); primary SRO for BDs and associated persons.

FINRA jurisdiction: investment banking (underwriting), OTC trading, exchange-listed trading, conduct of member firms and associated persons; SEC-delegated administration of qualification exams (e.g., SIE, Series 6, 7).
FINRA member firms may only do business with other FINRA members, with limited exceptions (e.g., bank in a municipal underwriting; foreign firm that is a member of its country's FINRA equivalent).
FINRA's Four Rulebooks: Conduct Rules, Code of Procedure (COP), Uniform Practice Code (UPC), Code of Arbitration (COA).
Conduct Rules: fair dealing, compensation, communications, sales practice violations.

Code of Procedure (COP): disciplinary process. Department of Enforcement (DOE) investigates and holds hearings; sanctions include suspension, expulsion, bar, fines, censure, any other appropriate action. FINRA has NO arrest powers.
COP Appeals Chain: DOE → National Adjudicatory Council (NAC) → SEC → Federal Appellate Courts.
Uniform Practice Code (UPC): technical aspects of securities transactions (good delivery, settlement dates, ex-dividend dates, accrued interest, etc.).

Code of Arbitration (COA): mandatory dispute resolution for MONETARY disputes between members and between members and associated persons; voluntary for customers (but customers usually agree via predispute arbitration clause in new account form). Arbitration decisions are FINAL AND BINDING — no appeal.
MSRB: primary SRO for municipal securities (debt AND non-debt municipal securities like 529 plans and ABLE accounts). MSRB writes rules but has NO enforcement authority.
MSRB rule enforcement: against banks → OCC, Federal Reserve, FDIC; against securities firms → SEC and FINRA. MSRB has NO authority over municipal issuers themselves.
Exchanges (e.g., NYSE) are both market centers AND SROs; regulate trading on the exchange; may delist or suspend trading on listed securities.
Order audit trail: the Consolidated Audit Trail (CAT) is the current audit-trail system (OATS was retired September 1, 2021).

RECORD RETENTION — Life of the Firm (Indefinite): partnership agreement, corporate charter/articles of incorporation, stock certificate books, board/partner meeting minutes, amendments to these records, organizational records (e.g., Form BD).

RECORD RETENTION — 6 Years: blotters (records of original entry — trades, securities receipts/deliveries, cash receipts/disbursements), general ledger, stock record, customer ledgers/statements, customer account records (new account form, margin agreement), designation of principals.

RECORD RETENTION — 4 Years (FINRA): written customer complaints (retained 4 years after resolution at the OSJ where the complaint originated). NOTE: SEC Rule 17a-4 requires only 3 years for complaints; most firms follow the stricter 4-year FINRA rule.

RECORD RETENTION — 3 Years: advertising, trial balances, U4/U5 and fingerprint cards (for terminated personnel), customer confirmations, order tickets, other ledgers (securities borrowed/loaned, money borrowed/loaned, dividends and interest received), list of every office, associated persons' compensation records, firm's compliance and procedures manuals.
Accessibility: For 3- and 6-year records, the most recent 2 years must be easily accessible (branch, OSJ, or headquarters).

Storage media: Digital storage permitted; must preserve records in a non-rewriteable, non-erasable format (WORM). SEC amended Rule 17a-4(f) in 2023 to permit an 'audit-trail alternative' to traditional WORM storage (Rel. 34-96034).
Definition of 'written' complaint is broad — includes letters, email, text, IM, tweets, social media posts. Verbal complaints have no recordkeeping standing.
rules: FINRA Conduct Rules — customer-facing fair dealing, communications, sales practices.
FINRA Code of Procedure — disciplinary process for rule violations.
FINRA Uniform Practice Code — technical/operational transaction rules.
FINRA Code of Arbitration — binding dispute resolution.
SEC Rule 17a-3 — required books and records to be created.
SEC Rule 17a-4 — record preservation periods and storage media requirements (amended 2023 to allow audit-trail alternative to WORM).
MSRB Rules — enforced by FINRA/SEC (securities firms) or OCC/Federal Reserve/FDIC (banks).
mnemonics: COP Appeals: 'DOE NACks SEC in Court' — DOE → NAC → SEC → Courts.
FINRA's 4 books: 'Cops Use Arbitration Codes' — Conduct, UPC, Arbitration, Code of Procedure.
Retention 'Life-6-4-3': Life-of-firm (foundational docs) → 6 yrs (customer & financial records) → 4 yrs (written complaints, FINRA) → 3 yrs (everything else).
MSRB: 'Makes rules, Skips Regulating, Banks/BDs enforce' — writes rules, no enforcement of its own.
Arbitration is FINAL — no appeal; COP rulings CAN be appealed.
